![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14218806/assets/21cf8b9a6a94900b68a565a2d0915ba849379a134009c37db64bd5ff1eea2ac7.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above? 

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,-{2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,-{2}^{+}}f(x)$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x)$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x)$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the limits in question. 

As $x$ approaches $-2$ from the left, the function value $f(x)$ approaches $y=2,$ and consequently

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-{2}^{-}}f(x)=2\,.
$$

As $x$ approaches $-2$ from the right, the function value $f(x)$ approaches $y=-2,$ and consequently

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-{2}^{+}}f(x)=-2\,.
$$

We cannot approach $x=1$ from the right because the function is not defined to the right of $x=1.$ Consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}\,.
$$

Similarly, we cannot approach $2$ from the left because the function is not defined to the left of $x=2.$ Consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x)=\text{DNE}\,.
$$

As $x$ approaches $1$ from the left, the function value $f(x)$ approaches $y=1,$ and consequently

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)=1\,.
$$

As $x$ approaches $2$ from the right, the function value $f(x)$ approaches $y=1,$ and consequently

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x)=1\,.
$$

Now, let's look at each statement in turn.

- I. ${lim}_{x\to \,-{2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,-{2}^{+}}f(x)$ becomes $2=-2,$ which is false.

- II. ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x)$ is false because neither one-sided limit exists.

- III. ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x)$ becomes $1=1,$ which is true.

Thus, only statement III is true.
